tolerance_html:
mechloop/tolerance/process.py holds, per process, the standard deviations the tolerance verifier built its 3000 simulated machines with. The sheets hold the fabricator to +/-2 standard deviations of the same figures, so a batch of parts inside the drawing tolerance is the population that was simulated. A part AT the limit everywhere is worse than what was simulated: the limits are not a licence to sit on them.

printing_html:
• Printer assumed by the manufacture verifier: build volume (220.0, 220.0, 220.0), nozzle 0.4 mm, layer 0.2 (the verifier default: the design does not declare one) mm.
  • Orientation: pinned per part in the design (print_up), listed below; the STL is already turned so the bed face is on Z = 0.
  • Walls and infill: not declared by the design. The verifier's mass and time estimate used: None.
  • The FEA load cases treat every printed part as solid, isotropic material. A part printed at 20 % infill is not the part that was analysed. For the parts with a load case (), print solid or accept that the factor of safety is unverified.
  • No threads in plastic, no heat-set inserts: every screw in a printed part runs into a steel nut (captive pockets and slots are in the models).
  • Printed clearance holes are drawn at ISO 273 medium + 0.2 mm FDM allowance (M2.5 3.1, M3 3.6, M4 4.7, M5 5.7, M6 6.8; +0.3 and a teardrop or flat top for a hole whose axis lies in the build plane): vertical holes print undersize. Starting values: print a coupon of M3 holes 3.4 to 3.8 in 0.1 mm steps on the printer that will make the parts, then set the allowance and the slicer's hole compensation (docs/DESIGN_GUIDELINES.md). Bearing seats and insert pockets are drawn to their own figures.

parts.name: nut_plate
parts.desc: Laser-cut 6061 nut plate on the carrier. How the bed is lifted: the T8 brass nut z_nut rides lead screw leadscrew. Its 22 mm flange is under this 9.525 mm plate and its 10.2 mm barrel goes up through the plate's 16.6 mm hole. The carrier's weight rests on the flange, so when the screw turns, the nut climbs it and lifts the plate (and the carrier and bed) with it; turned the other way, the nut goes down and the carrier follows it under its own weight. The M2.5 pin screw nut_pin (through a 5 mm aluminium sleeve, fixed in the flange) sits in a radial slot in the plate: it stops the nut turning with the screw while letting it float 2.8 mm sideways, so a screw that is not exactly where the plate's hole is does not push the carrier sideways. Nothing clamps the plate to the flange: gravity alone holds it down, which is why the nut-seating study (every nut keeps a positive load with the screws at opposite lead limits) matters. Pushed up: in normal running nothing pushes the bed upward (a nozzle crash pushes it down onto the flanges, and the inductive probe does not touch it), but a hand lifting the bed, or something trapped under the carrier while Z moves down, lifts the plate off the flange with no stop. It re-seats by itself up to about 9.7 mm of lift, while the pin's sleeve is still in its slot (the barrel stays in the hole to 10 mm); beyond that the nut can turn and must be lined up by hand before the bed is lowered onto it.

parts.name: z_nut_fr
parts.desc: T8 flanged brass nut, floating under nut_plate_fr. How the bed is lifted: the T8 brass nut z_nut_fr rides lead screw leadscrew_fr. Its 22 mm flange is under this 6.35 mm plate and its 10.2 mm barrel goes up through the plate's 16.6 mm hole. The carrier's weight rests on the flange, so when the screw turns, the nut climbs it and lifts the plate (and the carrier and bed) with it; turned the other way, the nut goes down and the carrier follows it under its own weight. The M2.5 pin screw nut_pin_fr (through a 5 mm aluminium sleeve, fixed in the flange) sits in a radial slot in the plate: it stops the nut turning with the screw while letting it float 2.8 mm sideways, so a screw that is not exactly where the plate's hole is does not push the carrier sideways. Nothing clamps the plate to the flange: gravity alone holds it down, which is why the nut-seating study (every nut keeps a positive load with the screws at opposite lead limits) matters. Pushed up: in normal running nothing pushes the bed upward (a nozzle crash pushes it down onto the flanges, and the inductive probe does not touch it), but a hand lifting the bed, or something trapped under the carrier while Z moves down, lifts the plate off the flange with no stop. It re-seats by itself up to about 6.5 mm of lift, while the pin's sleeve is still in its slot (the barrel stays in the hole to 10 mm); beyond that the nut can turn and must be lined up by hand before the bed is lowered onto it.

open_items.title: Bed probe on a thin spring-steel sheet: sensing distance unverified
open_items.known: Every probe figure (z_offset 3.0 mm, range [2.0, 4.0], face window [0.626, 3.374] mm) assumes the sensor switches at 5.0 mm, the maker's figure for a 1 mm iron target. The target here is PEI spring-steel print sheet 180 x 180 x 0.4 with magnetic base (TRONXY PEI180), 0.4 mm (a catalogue part) on its magnetic base. Basis recorded by the report: OMRON E2E data sheet CSM_E2E_DS_E_12_4: 5 mm +/-10 % on the standard iron target.

open_items.title: Lead screws stand in 608 bearings on their thread crests
open_items.known: Each catalogue screw is a plain threaded T8 bar, no machined journals: both 608s ride on the thread crests (the fit is 'catalogue fit, trusted', not simulated).
